lessons.title: The spectrum and the three divisions of EW
lessons.summary: Explain what the electromagnetic spectrum is and classify an activity by its purpose.

sections.heading: Why the spectrum matters
sections.text: The electromagnetic spectrum covers the full range of electromagnetic radiation. Radios, radars, and satellite navigation all depend on portions of it. The electromagnetic operational environment describes the electromagnetic conditions and activity relevant to an operation. Those conditions can affect whether systems work as intended.

sections.heading: Classify the activity by its purpose
sections.text: Electromagnetic warfare uses electromagnetic or directed energy to control use of the spectrum or affect an adversary. Electromagnetic attack (EA) acts against adversary capability. Electromagnetic protection (EP) protects friendly people, facilities, and equipment from harmful effects of spectrum use. Electromagnetic support (ES) detects or identifies emissions to inform decisions. More than one division can contribute to the same mission.

sections.heading: Read the doctrine
sections.text: Read the JP 3-85 Executive Summary and Chapter I overview. Look up EA, EP, ES, and EW in glossary Part II.

questions.prompt: Which three divisions make up EW?
questions.answer: Electromagnetic attack, electromagnetic protection, and electromagnetic support.

questions.prompt: An exercise team identifies an unexpected emission so staff can understand the environment. Which division matches that purpose?
A unit protects friendly equipment from harmful electromagnetic effects. Which division fits?

lessons.title: Spectrum management and interference
lessons.summary: Explain why organizations coordinate spectrum use and distinguish an observation from a cause.

sections.heading: Coordinate a shared resource
sections.text: Different users can need the same or overlapping parts of the spectrum. Spectrum management brings together planning, engineering, and administrative work so users can meet requirements under applicable rules. Frequency assignments and coordination help compatible users operate alongside each other.

sections.heading: Describe the symptom first
sections.text: Interference can arise from friendly systems, civilian activity, or other electromagnetic conditions. A brief failure during an exercise establishes a symptom. Staff can compare observations, check for conflicts, and record what remains unknown before drawing a conclusion about the cause.

sections.heading: Read the doctrine
sections.text: Read the introductory paragraphs of JP 3-85 Appendix A. Use the Army Communicator article's Collaboration Is Combat Power section to connect the concept to the Army spectrum manager role.

terms: Spectrum management — planning and coordination of spectrum use
Frequency assignment — authorized use of a frequency under specified conditions
EMI — electromagnetic interference that degrades system performance
Deconfliction — coordination to prevent incompatible activities from interfering with one another

questions.prompt: Two exercise teams request overlapping spectrum use. What staff function can assess the conflict?
What can you conclude from an unexplained interruption alone?
questions.answer: An interruption occurred. Its cause still needs evidence.
Early coordination gives staff time to identify conflicts and reconcile requirements before they affect other users.

lessons.title: How Army staff and EW units work together
lessons.summary: Identify what commanders, coordinating staffs, spectrum managers, and EW units contribute.

sections.heading: Who contributes what
sections.text: Commanders establish objectives and priorities. Staff integrate inputs from operations, intelligence, signal, and other functions into a common understanding. The spectrum manager helps reconcile spectrum requirements. EW personnel contribute expertise about electromagnetic conditions and EW capabilities relevant to the mission.

sections.heading: How the pieces fit
sections.text: Cyberspace electromagnetic activities (CEMA) provide an Army context for coordinating related work across the staff. The public Army Communicator overview describes spectrum managers collaborating with EW, cyber, intelligence, and operations staff. The ATP 3-12.4 preface identifies platoon leaders and platoon sergeants as its primary audience.

sections.heading: Read the doctrine
sections.text: Start with the ATP 3-12.4 preface for the publication's audience. Read Collaboration Is Combat Power for staff coordination, then use the FM 3-12 catalog entry to identify the current Army baseline.

terms: 25E — Army electromagnetic spectrum manager military occupational specialty
EW platoon — Army unit organized for electromagnetic warfare duties
Staff integration — coordination of inputs from different staff functions around common objectives

questions.prompt: Who establishes the unit's objectives and priorities?
Who helps reconcile spectrum-use requirements across staff functions?
questions.answer: The spectrum manager, working with stakeholders across the staff.

questions.prompt: Who is the primary audience for ATP 3-12.4?
questions.answer: EW platoon leaders and platoon sergeants.

lessons.title: How joint forces coordinate spectrum use
lessons.summary: Explain the relationship among the joint force commander, service components, and the joint electromagnetic spectrum operations cell.

sections.heading: A shared operating environment
sections.text: A joint force's components operate in a shared electromagnetic environment. Joint electromagnetic spectrum operations (JEMSO) bring together electromagnetic warfare and spectrum management so the force can prioritize, synchronize, and deconflict activities in support of joint objectives.

sections.heading: Coordinate across components
sections.text: Service components bring their requirements and subject-matter expertise. The joint electromagnetic spectrum operations cell (JEMSOC) helps coordinate activities for the joint force commander. Its work can include aligning requirements across components and addressing conflicts with partners.

sections.heading: Read the doctrine
sections.text: Read the JP 3-85 Executive Summary and Chapter II introduction. Compare the responsibilities discussed there with the opening Purpose and Summary of Changes in CJCSM 3320.01D.

terms: JEMSOC — joint electromagnetic spectrum operations cell
Service component — a service's organization participating in a joint force

questions.prompt: What two areas does JEMSO bring together?
What does the JEMSOC help the joint force commander do?
questions.answer: Coordinate and integrate joint electromagnetic spectrum operations.

questions.prompt: Two service components have conflicting spectrum requirements in a tabletop exercise. Why surface that conflict at joint level?
questions.answer: Joint coordination can reconcile conflicting demands across components and align them with the joint force commander's priorities.

lessons.title: Find and read the right publication
lessons.summary: Choose a doctrine source for a question and verify its title, date, and changes.

sections.heading: Start with a question
sections.text: For Army-level framing, find FM 3-12 in the Army Publishing Directorate (APD) record. Use the JP 3-85 Executive Summary and glossary for joint terminology. Use ATP 3-12.4's preface for the EW platoon audience and the ATP 6-02.70 catalog record for the Army spectrum management reference.

sections.heading: Verify the edition
sections.text: Check the publication number, title, basic edition date, and listed changes. A change sheet can carry a newer date than the cover. For example, APD lists ATP 3-12.3 with a January 2023 basic edition and two subsequent changes. Verify the APD record if a saved copy and the official listing differ.

sections.heading: Choose supplemental context
sections.text: ATP 3-01.81 provides context for counter-unmanned aircraft system operations. ATP 7-100.1 and ATP 7-100.3 provide separate operational environment references for Russian and Chinese ground forces. Use the covers and prefaces to identify each publication's scope before continuing.

terms: Basic edition — original issue date of the listed edition
Change — an issued update to a publication

questions.prompt: Which source provides the joint terminology and coordination framework?
questions.answer: JP 3-85, starting with its Executive Summary and glossary.

questions.prompt: Which source describes the EW platoon and names its primary audience?
A downloaded ATP has the correct title but only shows Change 1. What do you check?
questions.answer: Check the official APD record for the basic edition and any later changes. ATP 3-12.3 currently lists Change 2.
